Casks were marked with a merchant's device and identified by standard size - tun, pipe, butt, hogshead, barrel - rather than written labels, because most seamen could not read.

Beer was carried in preference to water because water in wood goes foul.

Gold in Virginia
Gold in Virginia.
MYTH: that Virginia held Spanish-style gold deposits.
The belief rested on promotional writing and analogy with Spanish Peru - not on any evidence from Virginia itself.
Too Many Gentlemen
Too Many Gentlemen.
A large share of the first colonists were gentlemen and their servants, who regarded manual farm labour as beneath their station - leaving very few willing or able to grow food.
The Colony's Fatal Composition
The Colony's Fatal Composition.
The combination of an unfounded expectation of gold and a workforce unwilling to farm meant the colony was poorly equipped to feed itself - a direct cause of the starvation that
followed.
What the Gentlemen Expected
What the Gentlemen Expected.
Many colonists expected to find wealth quickly and return home, rather than to build a permanent, self-feeding settlement.
The Roanoke Colony
The Roanoke Colony.
In fifteen eighty-seven over 100 English settlers - including women and children - were landed at Roanoke, off the Carolina coast.
It was a full colony, not a garrison.
Why Roanoke Was Abandoned
Why Roanoke Was Abandoned.
Governor John White sailed to England for supplies in fifteen eighty-seven; war with Spain (the Armada) commandeered every available ship, delaying his return until fifteen ninety.
What Was Found at Roanoke
What Was Found at Roanoke.
In fifteen ninety John White found the settlement empty: no bodies, no graves, no signs of battle, the houses dismantled in orderly fashion
, and 'CROATOAN' carved on a post - the name of a nearby island and people.

The Virginia Company
The Virginia Company.
A for-profit joint-stock company funded the colony.
Shareholders expected returns: precious metals, saleable commodities, and a hoped-for water passage through Virginia to Asia.
Colonists as Company Servants
Colonists as Company Servants.
Under the charter, colonists were the Company's employees for a seven-year term.
Land, stores, and produce belonged to the Company and were held in a common store, not owned by settlers.
Whim and Ledger
Whim and Ledger.
ANALYTIC: Roanoke was a Crown-backed venture undone by war; Jamestown was a joint-stock business whose survival depended on returns to investors.
Both left colonists dependent on decisions made three thousand miles away for reasons that had nothing to do with them.
Reading a Document's Purpose
Reading a Document's Purpose.
The charter's religious language was likely sincere AND served the venture's interests - lending legitimacy to settlement on land already inhabited.
Sources can be honest and self-serving simultaneously.
The Sealed Box
The Sealed Box.
The names of the colony's governing Council were sealed in a locked box, not to be opened until landfall - so no colonist knew who would command them during the crossing.
Profit or Perish
Profit or Perish.
Because the colony was a commercial venture, continued supply depended on producing something profitable.
No saleable cargo meant no incentive for investors to keep sending ships.
What the Charter Actually Says
What the Charter Actually Says.
The sixteen oh six charter claims land 'not now actually possessed by any Christian Prince or People' - excluding the Powhatan by definition; states a religious purpose; reserves
the King a fifth of all gold and silver; establishes a Council of thirteen; and grants English liberties to the colonists alone.
The Matchlock Caliver
The Matchlock Caliver.
The arm carried to Virginia in sixteen oh seven: a matchlock, fired by touching a lit slow match to powder in an open pan.
One or two shots a minute in trained hands.
Why the Match Matters
Why the Match Matters.
A matchlock is fired by a lit cord.
It must be kept glowing throughout loading, gives the firer away at night, and is nearly useless in rain or wind.
The Six Motions
The Six Motions.
Charge with powder, drop the ball, seat a wad, ram it home, prime the pan, present and give fire - all while keeping the slow match alight.
What the Piece Could Actually Do
What the Piece Could Actually Do.
A matchlock caliver would drive a ball through armour at a hundred paces, which is why every company carried them.
What it would not do is pick out one particular man at that distance: it is a smoothbore firing a ball deliberately cast under its own bore
, and past forty yards or so it is a guess.
That is why soldiers were drilled to fire together rather than to aim.
And it took the better part of a minute to load again.
Reach was never this weapon's problem at Jamestown.
The minute was.
The Seven Named in the Box
The Seven Named in the Box.
The Virginia Company sealed the names of the colony's seven councillors in a locked box, not to be opened until landfall.
For the whole voyage nobody knew who held authority.
Two of the seven were problems the moment the box was opened: George Kendall, who would be removed and executed within the year, and John Smith
, who was under arrest when his name was read out.
Overruled
Overruled.
The site was chosen by the president of the council, not by vote.
A colonist could be right about the ground and still be overruled - authority in the colony did not rest on evidence.

Four months and more at sea are behind you.
Land was descried at four this morning, and the ships are standing into the Chesapeake between two capes that had no English names yesterday, low green country on either hand
, while the gentlemen argue over where they will plant the fort.
Below deck, in the dark and the stink, men still trade the old rumours - of a colony that vanished, and of a Company that promised them gold.
You are hungry, and the provisions are stowed in the hold.
Question the crew - all three of them, until they have nothing left to tell you - and read the Charter that lies in the great cabin.
The scrivener sits with you only when you have done all four, and then he asks six questions drawn from a great many, some of them off a chart.
What is hidden in the hold is not required, but a man who has found it answers more easily.

“You've the green look of a first crossing.
Ask me quick - I'll not talk once the boatswain's about.”
Have Englishmen tried to settle Virginia before us?
I'd know what became of them.
“Aye.
Roanoke, twenty year gone.
Over a hundred souls - men, women, children among them - put ashore on an island inside the banks, south of where we are bound, in fifteen eighty-seven.
A proper colony, not a fort of soldiers.”
How long were we at sea?
It felt like a year.
“Four months and more, and six weeks of that in sight of Kent, with the wind in our teeth and not a mile made good.”
He jerks his chin at the daylight.
“It is behind you.
Land was called at four this morning.
Ask me about the country you are looking at.”
Will the Company pay us well once we're ashore?
“Pay?”
He barks a laugh.
“Ask the clerk about wages, boy - he keeps the papers.
Ask me about the country and what's already happened in it.”
I know English ships have worked this coast before.
Fishermen, privateers.
“They have, and every one of them sailed home again.”
He is unimpressed.
“Touching a coast is not the same as being PUT ASHORE on it and left.
That is the thing you ought to be asking me, but have it your way.”
Has England ever put families ashore in that country before - not soldiers, but households?
“Once, with families.
Roanoke, in fifteen eighty-seven, on an island off the banks south of where we are bound.
Above a hundred of them, women and children among them.”
He works his jaw.
“That is the whole difference, and nobody aboard sees it.
Soldiers you can fetch off again.
A colony has come to live.”
Has an English child ever been born in that country before now?
“One that I know of.
A girl, born on Roanoke in the August of '87, within a month of their landing - the first English child born in that country.
They christened her Virginia, after the place.”
He looks out at the water.
“Men do not carry a woman big with child three thousand mile across the sea to hold a fort for a season.
That was a colony.
They meant to stay, and to raise her there.”
Were the last Englishmen there soldiers sent to fight the Spanish?
“There were soldiers on that island once, aye.
A company of them, with a fort, and they gave it up and took ship home.”
He waves it away.
“You are not wrong, you are only behind.
I am speaking of the lot that came after.
Ask me who was put ashore then.”
That country is empty of people, is it not - nobody living there before us?
“Empty.”
He laughs, with nothing in it.
“I have been twice on that coast.
There are fields cleared down to the water, and smoke standing over the trees where the towns are, and more people in them than in the parish I was born in.”
He shakes his head.
“And Englishmen have been put ashore in that country before us.
Ask me about those.”
“You've the look of a man who wants the rest of it.
Go on.”
Why was such a colony left without supply for so long?
“Their governor, White, sailed home for supply that same year - left his own daughter and grandchild behind.
Then Spain came at England with the whole Armada, and every hull in the kingdom was pressed to the fight.
Three years he fought to get a ship back.
Three years.”
The Company must simply have forgotten them.
“Forgotten?”
“White near killed himself trying to get back.
It weren't forgetting.
Think what a war with Spain does to a kingdom's shipping, and ask me again.”
Surely they could have sailed home under their own sail?
“With what?
White took the only ship worth the name.
They'd a pinnace at best, and no stores for an ocean.”
He grunts.
“The question isn't why they stayed.
It's why nobody came.”
What was England busy with in those years that mattered more than a hundred colonists?
“Saving its own neck.
Word came that Spain meant to invade, and the Council laid a stay on shipping - not a hull to leave an English port.
Then the Armada came up the Channel in '88, and every ship that could carry a gun was wanted for the fight.”
He shrugs.
“A hundred souls on an island three thousand mile off do not weigh much against that.
They were still there, though.”
Did their own governor never try to fetch them help himself?
“Their governor was White, and try he did.”
He holds up two fingers.
“He got two small ships out of England in '88 - all he could get.
They went hunting prizes on the way, the way every ship did that year, and better-armed men fell on them and sent them home shot to pieces, never near that coast at all.”
His mouth goes thin.
“Two more years after that before he stood on the island.”
Ships are lost at sea all the time - perhaps the relief simply never made the crossing.
“One ship lost is ill luck.”
“Three years without one is a reason.
You are not wrong about the sea, but you have not asked what the reason was.”
Did White save himself and leave them to it?
“They sent him.
It was the colony's own doing - they wanted a man in England with a name to him, who would stand up and shout for supply.”
“He came back for them in the end.
What you want to ask is what kept him so long.”
England had no money to send a ship, I suppose.
“It weren't the purse that stopped it.”
He looks at you a moment.
“Money buys nothing when there is no hull to be had at any price.
It was the harbours that were empty.
Now think what England wanted with every ship she had in those years.”
“And when White finally set foot on that island again, in fifteen ninety -”
He stops, and spits over the rail.
What did he actually find there?
Bodies?
Ruin?
“Nothing.
No bodies.
No graves, no burned houses, no arrows in the palings.
The houses taken down neat and orderly, as if by men with time on their hands.
And one word cut into a post - CROATOAN.
The name of an island to the south, and of the people living on it.”
The Spanish had put them all to the sword, I'd wager.
“And left no bodies?
No burned timber, no broken palings?”
He looks at you flatly.
“The Spanish don't tidy up after a slaughter.
Whatever happened on that island, it weren't a massacre.
Ask me what was actually there.”
Then they starved where they stood.
“Starved men leave bones.
And they don't take their own houses apart plank by plank first.”
He taps the rail.
“That was an orderly leaving, not a dying.
Ask me plain what he found.”
Did they leave him any sign - anything cut or written where he would be sure to find it?
“One word, cut in a post at the entrance.
CROATOAN - an island to the south of there, and the people living on it.”
He holds up a finger.
“And here is the part men leave out.
Before ever he sailed they had agreed on a token between them: if they were driven off in distress, they should cut a cross above the name.
There was no cross.
No bodies, no graves, no burning - and no cross.”
Did the place look like men running, or men taking their time about it?
“Taking their time.”
He is certain of it.
“The houses were not knocked down.
They were taken to pieces and carried off.
And round the whole ground somebody had set up a fence of great trees, high and strong, made like a fort - and that went up after White sailed, for it was not there when he left.”
He knocks the rail with his knuckles.
“Frightened men do not build a wall and then unbuild their own houses.
Whatever moved them, it was not one night's terror.”
Did he dig about the place for whatever they left in the ground?
“He found his own chests dug up and spoiled.
Books torn out of their covers, maps and pictures rotted with the rain, armour eaten through with rust.”
“Somebody had been at them after the leaving - a good while, by the rot on the books.
That is furniture, boy.
Set the chests aside and look at the whole place, for that is where the answer is lying.”
Perhaps he came to the wrong island - three years is a long while to remember a coast.
“He had lived on that ground.
His own chests lay buried in it, and he found them broken open and spoiled.”
A flat look.
“It was the place.
What was wanting was the people - and the people are the question.”
“So.
You've heard the whole of it now.
What do you make of it?”
That what stranded them - no ship coming - is the very thing the Company's arithmetic promises us.
Ask the Company Clerk what happens if the colony turns no profit.
“Aye.”
He is quiet a moment, and looks at you properly.
“White could get no hull because England was at war.
We shall get none because there'll be nothing in the hold worth a merchant's while carrying home.
Different reason.
Same empty horizon.
You're the first man on this ship to say it to me.”
Roanoke and the Supply Problem
Roanoke and the Supply Problem.
ANALYTIC: Roanoke was lost partly because war with Spain stopped resupply.
Jamestown's resupply depended instead on the colony producing cargo worth shipping home.
Different causes - the same vulnerability: a settlement that cannot feed itself depends entirely on ships arriving.
That they likely went to live among the Croatoan - and that in truth nobody knows.
“That's the honest answer, and the rare one.”
He looks at you properly for the first time.
“Most men aboard have already settled it in their heads - savages did it, or Spaniards, or it was God's judgement.
Truth is we do not know.
And that's the thing that turns my stomach: a hundred English can vanish in that country and leave nothing behind but a word cut in a post.”
That it proves the natives of that country cannot be trusted.
“Does it?”
He frowns.
“There's no blood, no battle, and the word they left behind was the name of a people who'd been friendly to them.
You've leapt to a verdict the evidence won't carry.
Try again, and stay with what was found.”
That it's a tale sailors tell to frighten green men.
“I have stood on that island.”
His face closes.
“It is no tale.
But go on - tell me what the evidence says, not what's comfortable to believe.”
Rather than guess where they went, tell me what the evidence rules out.
“Now that is the right end of it.”
He leans on the rail.
“No bodies on that ground, so it was no slaughter.
No bones, so they did not starve where they stood.
No char, no broken palings, nothing thrown down - so it was neither stormed nor burnt.
Everything gone from that place was carried, and by the look of it carried by them.”
He is quiet a moment.
“What is left standing is a word cut in a post.
That is a direction, not an answer, and I'll not make it one.”
What would a man have to find, even now, to settle it one way or the other?
That is the question nobody puts.”
He thinks about it longer than you expect.
“One of them living, and able to say it.
Or a child of theirs grown, in that country, with English on his tongue.
Or bones a man could swear were English, in ground somebody could name.”
He turns his hands over.
“Short of that we have a word on a post and our own wanting.
Mind which is which.”
Did nobody ever sail down to Croatoan and ask them?
“He meant to.
The weather came on foul, the cables parted, the anchors were lost, and the ship stood away for the islands to the south.”
He spits over the rail.
“No ship ever came at that island to ask.
Some tried, in the years after.
None of them made that ground.
That is not an answer - that is a hole where the answer should be.”
Nobody knows, so one guess is as good as another.
“Is it?”
“Then you have thrown away everything I told you and kept the shrug.
Some tales that ground will carry and some it will not.
Sort them, and come back to me.”
If we cannot know what happened, then it is no use to us.
“No use?”
He looks away down the deck.
“We know a hundred were landed.
We know no ship came for three years.
We know a man came back to an empty island.”
He turns back to you.
“That is a deal of use to men bound for the same coast.
Do not throw away what you have because you cannot have all of it - now count me up what we do know.”
“You have had the whole of it from me.
Roanoke, and what it means.
Go and think on it.”
“You listen before you decide.
That's rarer at sea than you'd think.”

“Mind the papers.
This charter is worth rather more than your life, in the Company's estimation.”
Who actually paid for this voyage, and what do they expect in return?
“Investors.
Dozens of them, pooling coin into a joint-stock company - each buys a share, each takes a share of whatever comes home.
They expect return: gold, silver, timber, sassafras, pitch, anything that sells in London.
And a water passage through this country to the South Sea, and so to the riches of Asia.”
The King paid for it, did he not?
“The King granted the charter.
He did not open his purse.”
The clerk almost smiles.
“Not a penny of Crown money is in these hulls.
Ask me again - who actually put up the coin?”
We sail for God and for England's glory, surely.
“It says so in the preamble, and I'd not call it a lie.”
He turns the page.
“But read on, to what the shareholders are promised.
Then ask me your question again.”
What would a river running through to the South Sea be worth to the men who paid?
“Everything.
It is written into their instructions - find a river that runs far into the land, and follow it up.”
He sets the pen down.
“This is a joint-stock company: many men buying shares, pooling the coin, dividing whatever comes home.
Gold would please them well enough.
But a short road through to the South Sea, and so to Asia, is a toll every merchant in Europe must pay us, year on year, for ever.
That is the great prize.
Gold is only the one they talk of in taverns.”
Someone is out of purse for my biscuit - who is it, and what do they want back?
“Out of purse.
Somebody always is.”
“Learn the two words while you are here.
The men who venture their money are called adventurers.
You venture your person, and so you are a planter.
The adventurers bought shares in a joint-stock - many men, many shares, and every share owed a part of whatever comes home.”
He turns the book toward you.
“Your biscuit is written on this page as a cost against that.
Costs are expected to earn.”
London merchants paid for it, I suppose, and they want gold for their trouble.
“Merchants, and gentlemen, and men who have never stood on a deck in their lives - that is what a joint-stock is for.
Many hands, many shares.”
He does not look up.
“As for gold, it stands first on their list and is not the whole of it.
Timber.
Pitch.
Sassafras.
A passage to Asia.
You have the beginning of the thing, which is more than the deck has.”
So this is a place for poor men to start a new life away from England?
“A refuge is a place men run to.”
He looks up.
“Nobody runs toward a coast with no Englishman standing on it and no crop in the ground.
Most of these men were sought out and their passage paid, and something is expected back from every one of them.”
He dips the pen.
“Ask me who paid, and what he expects for it.”
We came for freedom of religion, did we not?
That is what I was told.
“You are thinking of some congregation that took ship to be let alone.
This is not one.”
He turns the book so you can see the names.
“Gentlemen.
Labourers.
Carpenters.
A barber.
Entered one by one, and not a man of them entered out of a church that turned him out - they were gathered by men of business.”
He turns it back.
“The paper does speak of religion, and I will come to that if you stay by me.
Ask me first what those men of business were promised.”
“You've read further than most.
Ask on, while I've the light.”
Then what am I under this charter - a settler with land of my own?
“You are a servant of the Company.
Five years.
The land is theirs, the stores are theirs, the very shirt on your back was bought on their account.
What you dig or grow goes into a common magazine and is doled back out.
You will own nothing in Virginia for five years - if you live five years.”
The King's orders of November sixteen oh six, issued under the charter, bound the colonists to work in one common stock for their first five years.
Land, stores, and produce were held for the venture in common storehouses, not owned by settlers.
So each man is granted his own plot on arrival?
“Granted?”
He taps the page hard.
“Nothing is granted.
Everything is the Company's.
You are labour, not landowner.
Read the clause again and put the question to me properly.”
At least we'll be free men once ashore.
“Free to work where you are told.
There is a Council named in a sealed box we mayn't open until landfall - you'll not even choose who commands you.”
“'Free' is not the word this document uses.”
If I break ground and raise a field of corn in Virginia, whose corn is it?
“Not yours.
The land is the Company's, the seed is the Company's, the spade in your hand was bought on their account - and so is the corn.”
“It goes into a common store and is doled back out by measure: the same measure to the man who grew it and the man who stood and watched him.
Five years of that.
You are their servant, not a settler, and you will own nothing in Virginia until the term is out - if you live the term.”
What am I paid for these five years, and when do I see it?
“Nothing counted into your hand.”
He says it without softening.
“You are fed and clothed out of the common store while the term runs, and that is your wage.
At the end there is talk of a division - land parcelled out, a share of the stock to the planters.”
He taps the desk.
“Talk.
I have not got it in front of me on a page.
What I have got on a page is the five years, and the Company's orders for how you are to spend them.”
They paid my passage and take the whole risk, so five years seems a fair bargain.
“They did pay it, and that is why the term is long.
You have that much right.”
He allows it with a small nod.
“But a bargain is written by whoever holds the pen, and it was not yours.
While it runs you own nothing and you go where you are sent.”
He straightens the papers.
“Half an answer, honestly got.”
If the terms are poor, a man can simply quit and work for himself.
“Quit and walk where?”
“There is an ocean behind you and five years in front of you.
This is a contract, not a humour to be got over.”
He waits.
“Now put it to me properly, and ask what you are.”
